title: Find resellers selling below your MAP price every day with Python
author: Martin Petrov
summary: If you sell a product through other shops, you need to know which of them list it below your minimum advertised price (MAP), and you need to know it the day it happens, not at the end of the month. This is part 3 of a small series. In part 1 I compared one product's price across stores, and in part 2 I added a change mode that returns only offers whose price or stock moved. This post adds the MAP check I built on top of it this week: give it your MAP and it flags every offer below it, with the gap in money and in percent. Real output from today (2026-11-14) is below, plus the limits. Why the usual approach hurts Most small brands check MAP like this: Someone opens 20 to 200 reseller pages in a browser, once a week if there is time. They copy prices into a spreadsheet, some in USD, some in EUR or GBP. They compare each one with the MAP column by hand. A reseller drops the price on Monday, and the brand finds out on Friday, after other resellers have already matched it. A script helps, but then you own the scraper, the currency conversion, the per-product MAP table and the "what changed since yesterday" logic. That last part is the one that breaks. What the tool does I built the Cheapest Price Finder on Apify. You give it product page URLs from any stores. It reads the real price from each page's structured data (JSON-LD offers, Shopify product data, meta price tags), converts everything to one currency with daily ECB rates and sorts the offers from cheapest to most expensive. The MAP check adds three inputs: mapPrice : your MAP, in the convertTo currency. mapPrices (optional): a different MAP per product URL, as {url: price} . It overrides mapPrice for that URL. onlyChanged + monitorId (from part 2): return only new or changed offers, so a daily run is quiet unless something moved. Every row then gets mapPrice , belowMap (true/false), mapGap (how far below MAP, in money; negative means above MAP) and mapGapPercent . RUN_SUMMARY.mapCheck lists belowMapCount and belowMapUrls , so one key tells you whether today needs attention. Step 1: get a token Create a free Apify account and copy your token from Console (Settings, API and Integrations): export APIFY_TOKEN = your_token_here Step 2: one run with curl For the demo I used the AeroPress Original at four coffee shops. I am not the brand and I do not know AeroPress's real MAP, so I picked a made-up MAP of $42, and for one store a separate MAP of $49.95 to show the per-URL override: curl -X POST "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/martin10291~cheapest-price-finder/run-sync-get-dataset-items?token=$APIFY_TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"productUrls": [ "https://www.vervecoffee.com/products/aeropress-coffee-brewer", "https://www.intelligentsia.com/products/aeropress", "https://www.espressoparts.com/products/aeropress-coffee-maker", "https://www.stumptowncoffee.com/products/aeropress"], "convertTo": "USD", "mapPrice": 42, "mapPrices": {"https://www.stumptowncoffee.com/products/aeropress": 49.95}}' Real output (2026-11-14, run took 4.6 s) store price availability mapPrice belowMap mapGap mapGapPercent vervecoffee.com 39.95 USD InStock 42 true 2.05 4.9 intelligentsia.com 40.00 USD OutOfStock 42 true 2.00 4.8 espressoparts.com 44.95 USD InStock 42 false -2.95 -7.0 stumptowncoffee.com 46.00 USD InStock 49.95 true 3.95 7.9 And the summary from the same run: "mapCheck" : { "belowMapCount" : 3 , "belowMapUrls" : [ "https://www.vervecoffee.com/products/aeropress-coffee-brewer" , "https://www.intelligentsia.com/products/aeropress" , "https://www.stumptowncoffee.com/products/aeropress" ] , "mapPrice" : 42.0 , "perUrlPrices" : 1 , "currency" : "USD" } Note the Intelligentsia row: it is below MAP but out of stock. Whether that counts as a violation is your policy, so the tool reports availability and leaves the decision to you. Step 3: the same in Python, as a daily watch import os import requests ACTOR = "martin10291~cheapest-price-finder" URL = f "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/{ACTOR}/run-sync-get-dataset-items" RESELLERS = [ "https://www.vervecoffee.com/products/aeropress-coffee-brewer" , "https://www.intelligentsia.com/products/aeropress" , "https://www.espressoparts.com/products/aeropress-coffee-maker" , "https://www.stumptowncoffee.com/products/aeropress" , ] def map_violations ( map_price , per_url = None ) : body = { "productUrls" : RESELLERS , "convertTo" : "USD" , "mapPrice" : map_price , "mapPrices" : per_url or { } , "onlyChanged" : True , # only new or changed offers "monitorId" : "aeropress-map" , # keeps yesterday's prices for you } r = requests . post ( URL , params = { "token" : os . environ [ "APIFY_TOKEN" ] } , json = body , timeout = 300 ) r . raise_for_status ( ) return [ row for row in r . json ( ) if row . get ( "belowMap" ) ] if __name__ == "__main__" : for row in map_violations ( 42 ) : print ( f '{row["store"]}: {row["price"]} {row["currency"]} ' f '({row["mapGapPercent"]}% below MAP, {row["availability"]}, ' f 'change: {row["changeType"]})' ) With onlyChanged , the first run returns every offer once as new . I ran it twice today with MAP $39.95 and the same monitorId : Run 1 (6.5 s): 4 rows, all changeType: "new" , belowMapCount: 0 . Run 2 (5.2 s): 0 rows saved, summary "unchanged": 4 . So on a normal day your script prints nothing. On the day a reseller cuts the price, you get one row with changeType: "priceDrop" , previousPrice , priceChange and the MAP gap together. Step 4: schedule it The simplest way, no server: Open the actor page , paste your reseller URLs, set mapPrice , tick "Only changed offers" and type a Monitor ID. Save it as a Task and add a schedule, e.g. every day at 07:00. Optional: connect the dataset to Slack, email or Google Sheets with Apify integrations, or add a webhook on "run succeeded". Or run the Python file from your own cron: 0 7 * * * /usr/bin/python3 /home/me/map_watch.py >> /home/me/map.log 2>&1 Without an Apify account The MAP check (not the change mode) also works through plain HTTP APIs with one key: API.market , free plan to test. radarbg.com , my own site, 100 free calls a month with one key for all my APIs. curl -X POST https://radarbg.com/v1/cheapest-price-finder \ -H 'X-API-Key: YOUR_KEY' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"productUrls": ["https://www.vervecoffee.com/products/aeropress-coffee-brewer", "https://www.espressoparts.com/products/aeropress-coffee-maker"], "convertTo": "USD", "mapPrice": 42}' I tested this path today too: the same two rows came back with belowMap true and false. onlyChanged and monitorId are switched off on these APIs on purpose: the remembered prices would live in my account and be shared by every caller with the same URLs. Keep yesterday's rows yourself there, or use the Apify actor for the built-in change feed. Honest limits Big marketplaces often block automated requests. Amazon, Walmart and Best Buy frequently answer with a bot-check page. The tool does not bypass that; such pages land in RUN_SUMMARY.failed and are not charged. Brand stores and independent shops (Shopify, WooCommerce, Magento, BigCommerce) work best. It reads the listed price only : no coupons, cart discounts or shipping. A reseller who hides the real price in the cart will not show up. You choose the URLs. It does not find your resellers for you or match products; gtin , sku and brand in each row help you check. Pages that build the price only with JavaScript and publish no product data return "no price found". It does not contact anyone. It tells you who is below MAP; what you do next is up to you. Price On Apify it costs $3.00 per 1,000 saved results. With onlyChanged , unchanged offers are not saved and not billed, so 50 resellers checked daily cost nothing for results on a quiet day. Apify's free plan includes a small monthly credit, enough to try it. On API.market and radarbg.com there are free plans to test first. Wrap-up I built this because MAP checks are the same price scrape plus one comparison, and the comparison is what people end up doing by hand. Now one field does it. If you manage a brand with resellers, try it on Apify with 3 to 5 of your reseller pages. How many reseller pages would your daily list have? If a page returns "no price found", post the URL in the comments and I will look at it.

title: I built a Casablanca Stock Exchange terminal as a highschool senior
author: Adam Elfaqir
summary: I'm a 2ème bac student in Fès, Morocco, and I want a career in finance. Following the Casablanca Stock Exchange meant jumping between slow, scattered sites, so I built the screen I wanted: SAHM Terminal, a free terminal with live charts, a sector heat map, company pages, market news and a DCF valuation tool, in French and English. Live: https://sahm-terminal.vercel.app The stack Backend: Python and FastAPI serving JSON under /api/v1, plus the static front end. Front end: vanilla JavaScript, no framework, a hash router and function keys (F1 to F10) like a real terminal. Charts: TradingView Lightweight Charts for historical data, plus embedded market-data widgets for live quotes and the heat map. Tests: 113 pytest tests. Hosting: Vercel's free plan. The hard part: price history Historical prices come as exchange exports, one file per instrument. Raw prices are misleading when a company splits its shares: the price suddenly falls by half and a chart shows a crash that never happened. The pipeline detects splits, adjusts earlier prices, and keeps the original files untouched so any adjustment can be checked. A refresh script merges new exports into the existing history. The valuation tool The DCF screen estimates what a company could be worth from the cash it may generate in the future. The result depends entirely on the assumptions you enter, so the app labels it as an educational estimate and never as a recommendation. What went wrong I got the licence question wrong at first: historical exchange data can have redistribution conditions. I wrote to the exchange and am still waiting for an answer, and I will change anything they ask. Free hosting that runs Python without a credit card is hard to find. Vercel's FastAPI support worked after I told it where my app lived. Getting people to try it is a different job from building it. Feedback If you follow the Moroccan market, or you build data products, tell me what's missing. Contact: sahmterminal1@gmail.com

title: Do your tests really catch bugs? / Seus testes pegam erro de verdade?
author: Arthur Figueiredo
summary: I measured this together with Claude, ran research and tests, and built a garden about whether tests really catch bugs. The idea is simple: a test can pass and still be weak. To find out how weak, I broke the code on purpose and counted how many bugs the tests let through. Then I did the same for each step of my AI workflow, from the spec (the text that describes what the code should do) to the commit. In the garden, each step has its own number, and the ideas that didn't pay off are there too. There is one note just for what I still don't know, because the study is small, comes from a few projects, and nobody outside has checked it. And there is a step-by-step to repeat the measurement on your own project. "A digital garden is a site of linked notes that the author keeps tending over time. It accepts unfinished notes and shows it, with a badge for how well each one is proven." If you want to take a look: Digital-Garden 🇧🇷 Eu medi isso junto com o Claude, fiz pesquisas e testes, e criei um jardim sobre se os testes pegam erro de verdade. A ideia é simples: um teste pode passar e ainda assim ser fraco. Para saber o quanto, estraguei o código de propósito e contei quantos erros os testes deixaram passar. Depois fiz o mesmo com cada passo do meu fluxo de trabalho com IA, da spec (o texto que descreve o que o código deve fazer) até o commit. No jardim, cada passo tem o seu número, e as ideias que não compensaram também estão lá. Tem uma nota só com o que eu ainda não sei, porque o estudo é pequeno, vem de poucos projetos e ninguém de fora conferiu. E tem um passo a passo para repetir a medida no seu projeto. "Jardim digital é um site de notas ligadas entre si, que o autor continua cuidando com o tempo. Ele aceita nota inacabada e mostra isso, com um selo de quanto cada uma está provada." Se quiser olhar: Digital-Garden

title: a2claude Is Now a2acode: Any ACP Coding Agent Behind A2A
author: kt
summary: In June I shipped a2claude , which put Claude Code behind A2A so another agent could hand it coding work. It drove Claude through the Claude Agent SDK. Two weeks later I added a second backend that speaks Zed's Agent Client Protocol instead. ACP agents already report their work as structured session/update messages: tool calls, diffs, plans, permission requests. Those map almost one to one onto what a2claude was already sending over A2A. Once that worked, Claude Code was one launch command among several, and the name was wrong. It's a2acode now. Source: https://github.com/kanywst/a2acode Install: uvx a2acode serve (PyPI), or ghcr.io/kanywst/a2acode If ACP and A2A are new to you, I mapped them out in Mapping MCP, A2A, and ACP . This post skips that. Picking the agent uvx a2acode serve --cwd ./project # Claude Code, the default uvx a2acode serve --agent codex --cwd ./project uvx a2acode serve --agent gemini --cwd ./project uvx a2acode serve --agent-command "npx -y some-other-acp-agent" The presets are three lines in backends/acp.py , all launched through npx : @zed-industries/claude-agent-acp , @zed-industries/codex-acp , @google/gemini-cli --acp . Each agent picks up its own credential from the server's environment. The callers on the A2A side never see which one is running. The gemini preset only works on organization Code Assist plans. Google stopped serving the Gemini CLI to consumer accounts in June 2026, so on a personal account it fails before ACP or a2acode get involved. A run, over ACP I don't have keys for all three, so the output below comes from the repo's test agent ( tests/fake_agent.py ). It's a real ACP agent over stdio, the same handshake and session lifecycle, and each keyword in the prompt makes it exercise one part of the protocol. The server doesn't know it's a test. uv run a2acode serve --agent-command "python tests/fake_agent.py" --cwd ./ws --port 9177 uv run a2acode call "plan then edit then boom" --url http://localhost:9177/ task 229322b0-0e78-42a1-802d-3a117c59fd92 context 3c0fd964-fd51-4fe1-a694-bcc1044b9ce6 [thinking] considering [plan] - [x] look - [>] fix · Write calc.py [calc.py] --- a/calc.py +++ b/calc.py @@ -1 +1 @@ -a +b · ✓ Write calc.py · Run tests · ✗ Run tests: 2 tests failed turn 1: done [completed] On the A2A side, the reasoning is a thinking artifact, separate from the answer. The plan is a plan artifact that gets replaced as steps move. The diff is its own named artifact, and each tool call and its outcome arrive as working status updates. A caller can tell "the tests failed" apart from "the agent said the tests failed". All of that mapping lives in executor.py . Backends emit a fixed set of events and never import the A2A SDK, and the executor never imports an agent SDK. The ACP backend, the Claude SDK backend and an offline echo backend all go through the same mapping. Permission prompts go to the caller When the agent asks for permission, the task pauses in input-required and waits for the caller: $ a2acode call "ask" --url http://localhost:9177/ task a55854f6-f1df-4afc-9a2f-88fc702c03bf context a53af302-25f7-48c9-92ad-7866536dd94b [thinking] considering turn 1: [input-required] Permission requested for rm -rf /: rm -rf / options, answered as "option:<id>": 'ok' ['allow_once'] 'Allow' 'no' ['reject_once'] 'Deny' reply: a2acode call "allow" --task a55854f6-f1df-4afc-9a2f-88fc702c03bf --context a53af302-25f7-48c9-92ad-7866536dd94b --request 4a2afbaabfb64856901489a94d258644 --url http://localhost:9177/ (or "deny" to refuse) The agent process stays parked inside session/request_permission until an answer arrives on the same task: $ a2acode call "no, not on my machine" --task a55854f6-... --context a53af302-... --request 4a2afbaa... permission=no done [completed] Only a whole-message allow , yes , y , ok , approve , accept or grant approves ( _ALLOW_WORDS in executor.py ). Anything else denies, so the caller can answer in plain prose without accidentally approving something. The prose itself doesn't reach an ACP agent, though. ACP's permission response only has room for the chosen option, which is why the agent above only saw no . The Claude SDK backend does pass the words along, so no, run pytest -x instead redirects the turn there. The --request id ties an answer to one prompt. A run often pauses again right after you answer, and a retried request shouldn't approve a tool call the caller never saw. Terminals go through the same gate a2acode implements ACP's terminal capability, so the agent can ask the server to run a build or a test. ACP doesn't require an agent to ask permission before terminal/create , so if I had just advertised the capability, agents would have had a way to run commands without going through the gate. Instead every terminal/create gets the same pause, with the full command line: $ a2acode call "shell" --url http://localhost:9177/ ... [input-required] Permission requested for Terminal: …/.venv/bin/python -c 'print('"'"'from the terminal'"'"')' $ a2acode call "allow" --task bf667ad8-... --context 0e39fb1a-... --request 53a0a493... shell said from the terminal done [completed] (I shortened the interpreter path.) An approved command is not sandboxed. It runs as the server's user, and the only environment variables it inherits are PATH , HOME , LANG , TMPDIR , TERM , SHELL , USER , TZ and LC_* ( backends/terminal.py ), so the provider API key the server holds doesn't leak into it. The approval is where the security decision happens, so run the server as a user whose files you'd be fine with any approved command reading. Follow-up turns reuse the process The A2A contextId maps to the agent session, and the ACP backend keeps one agent process alive per context. The test agent counts turns per process: $ a2acode call "hello" context 9f0f6844-b74e-4ee6-adb5-5b77a50ab4c1 turn 1: done [completed] $ a2acode call "again" --context 9f0f6844-b74e-4ee6-adb5-5b77a50ab4c1 turn 2: done [completed] The second call goes to the same process, so there's no npx launch, no handshake, no session/load . If a new process does have to resume a session and the agent doesn't support session/load , the turn runs fresh and a status update says so. Pretending to remember would be worse. Discovery The agent card at /.well-known/agent-card.json lists A2A 1.0 and 0.3 interfaces (JSON-RPC and HTTP+JSON) on the same URL, so clients built on a v0.3 SDK can still find the server and run tasks. --sign-key signs the card with JWS. --auth-token-file requires a bearer token on every request except the card fetch. What I checked 223 tests pass on my machine ( uv run pytest ). Everything in this post was run against the test ACP agent, not against Claude Code, Codex or Gemini. The README says the full mapping has been checked end to end against real Claude. Source and issues: https://github.com/kanywst/a2acode

title: How do you calculate how much VRAM an LLM needs?
author: Viswaretas Kotra
summary: To serve an LLM, add the weights (parameters x bytes per parameter at your precision) to the KV cache (2 x layers x key-value heads x head size x bytes x tokens in flight), then divide by 0.92 for the headroom a serving engine keeps. Nodus turns that number into hardware: set minMemory on a Job and it runs on an accelerator with at least that much memory, such as an A100 80 GB listed at $1.090/hr on the Nodus pricing page. For Llama 3.1 8B in BF16 serving 32 requests of 8,192 tokens, the sum is 16.06 + 34.36 = 50.42 GB, about 55 GB of GPU, so an 80 GB card fits and a 48 GB card does not. This post is the general method. Every input comes from a model's config.json and its checkpoint files on Hugging Face, which we read on November 14, 2026. If you only care about one model size, our answer for 70B models goes deeper on that case. If you are training and hitting out-of-memory errors, the CUDA OOM guide breaks down training memory. We use decimal gigabytes throughout. What is the formula for LLM VRAM? Serving memory has three parts, and only one of them grows with traffic. weights = parameters x bytes per parameter KV cache = 2 x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes per value x tokens in flight GPU needed = (weights + KV cache) / 0.92 The weights are fixed once you pick a precision. The KV cache scales with every token of every request held at once. The 0.92 is the share of GPU memory that vLLM claims by default through --gpu-memory-utilization ; the rest covers the CUDA context and anything else on the card. "Tokens in flight" means prompt plus generated tokens, summed over concurrent requests. Thirty-two chats of 8,192 tokens each are 262,144 tokens in flight. How much memory do the weights take at FP16, FP8 and INT4? Start from 2 bytes per parameter for FP16 or BF16, 1 byte for FP8 and half a byte for INT4, then expect the quantized versions to come out larger. We summed the safetensors files of public checkpoints to see by how much: Model Parameters BF16 FP8 INT4 (AWQ) KV cache per token KV for 32,768 tokens Llama 3.1 8B 8.03 B 16.06 GB 9.08 GB 5.73 GB 0.131 MB 4.29 GB Qwen3-8B 8.19 B 16.38 GB 9.44 GB 6.10 GB 0.147 MB 4.83 GB Qwen3-32B 32.76 B 65.52 GB 34.32 GB 19.33 GB 0.262 MB 8.59 GB Llama 3.3 70B 70.55 B 141.11 GB 72.67 GB 39.77 GB 0.328 MB 10.74 GB Checkpoints used: RedHatAI FP8 and hugging-quants AWQ for Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen's own FP8 and AWQ releases (and their 32B FP8 and 32B AWQ versions), and the RedHatAI FP8 and casperhansen AWQ builds of Llama 3.3 70B. KV columns assume a BF16 cache. Sizes summed November 14, 2026. 4-bit cuts the weights to roughly a quarter on big models, but only to about a third on 8B ones. The gap comes from layers that stay at 16 bits plus the quantization scales. We can rebuild the Llama 3.1 8B numbers exactly. Its embedding and output layers each hold 128,256 x 4,096 parameters, 1.05 billion together, and both quantized checkpoints keep them at 16 bits (2.10 GB). The other 6.98 billion parameters cost 6.98 GB at FP8, which gives 9.08 GB. At INT4 they cost 3.49 GB, plus one 16-bit scale and one 4-bit zero point per group of 128 weights (the checkpoint's group_size is 128), or 0.14 GB. That totals 5.73 GB, matching the files. So the effective bytes per parameter were 1.13 at FP8 and 0.71 at INT4 for Llama 3.1 8B, but 1.03 and 0.56 for Llama 3.3 70B, where the embeddings are a smaller share. When a checkpoint exists, use its file size. When it does not, these four models suggest about 1.1 and 0.7 bytes for 8B-class models and 1.05 and 0.6 for 32B and up. Mixture-of-experts models follow the same rule with total parameters, not active ones. Every expert has to sit in memory even though each token uses a few. How do you calculate the KV cache from config.json? Read four fields: num_hidden_layers , num_key_value_heads , head_dim (or hidden_size / num_attention_heads when it is missing) and the cache precision. Llama 3.1 8B has 32 layers, 8 key-value heads and a head size of 128 in its config (a public mirror of Meta's gated file), so one token costs 2 x 32 x 8 x 128 x 2 bytes = 131,072 bytes. The key-value head count is where people go wrong. Llama 3.1 8B has 32 query heads but only 8 key-value heads, a design called grouped-query attention (GQA). Plugging in 32 heads gives 524,288 bytes per token, four times too much. The same mistake on Qwen3-32B's config (64 layers, 64 query heads, 8 key-value heads) turns 262,144 bytes into 2,097,152, eight times too much. For Qwen3-8B (36 layers, 32 query heads, 8 key-value heads) it is 147,456 versus 589,824 bytes, and for Llama 3.3 70B (80 layers, 64 query heads, 8 key-value heads) it is 327,680 versus 2,621,440. Reading the query head count instead of num_key_value_heads overstates the cache 4x to 8x. Two cases need a different formula. Models with multi-head latent attention, such as DeepSeek V3, cache a compressed vector per layer instead of per-head keys and values. Models with sliding-window layers only keep the window on those layers. For both, read the model card before trusting the generic formula. You can also halve the cache by storing it in FP8 with vLLM's --kv-cache-dtype fp8 , described on the same engine arguments page . Check quality on your own evaluations first. How much extra memory does the runtime need? Plan on the 8% that vLLM leaves free by default, and treat the result as a floor. At startup vLLM also runs a profiling pass and sets aside the peak activation memory from inside its 92% before sizing the cache, so real cache room comes out a little smaller than our arithmetic. The engine logs the KV cache size it actually got, in tokens, so read that line on the first launch and compare it with your estimate. Other runtimes differ. A plain Hugging Face generate() loop without a paged cache wastes more memory per request, so leave more room there. Worked example: does Llama 3.1 8B fit on a 48 GB GPU? Not in BF16 at 32 concurrent 8,192-token requests, and here is the check. Tokens in flight are 32 x 8,192 = 262,144. The KV cache is 262,144 x 131,072 bytes = 34.36 GB. Weights plus cache are 16.06 + 34.36 = 50.42 GB, and 50.42 / 0.92 = 54.80 GB. Re-checking the other way: a 48 GB card gives 48 x 0.92 = 44.16 GB to the engine, 6.26 GB short of 50.42. An 80 GB card gives 73.60 GB, which leaves 23.18 GB of slack. There are two ways to stay on 48 GB. An FP8 cache halves the KV term to 17.18 GB, so the total becomes 33.24 GB and the GPU needed is 36.13 GB, well inside 44.16. FP8 weights alone are not enough: 9.08 + 34.36 = 43.44 GB leaves 0.72 GB, too little once activations take their share. At real concurrency the cache, not the weights, decides the GPU: here it is twice the size of the model. Which GPU size fits your model? Take the smallest GPU class whose memory x 0.92 is at least weights plus cache. This is the rule we use, with the GPUs the Nodus pricing page lists in each class: GPU memory Usable at 0.92 GPUs on the Nodus pricing page, listed price per hour Example that fits, cache room left 24 GB 22.08 GB RTX 3090 $0.180, RTX 4090 $0.290, L4 $0.430 Llama 3.1 8B BF16, 6.02 GB (about 45,900 tokens) 48 GB 44.16 GB RTX A6000 $0.333, RTX 6000 Ada $0.743, L40S $0.793 Qwen3-32B INT4, 24.83 GB (about 94,700 tokens) 80 GB 73.60 GB A100 80 GB $1.090, H100 SXM $2.600 Llama 3.3 70B INT4, 33.83 GB (about 103,200 tokens) 96 GB 88.32 GB RTX PRO 6000 $1.350 Llama 3.3 70B INT4, 48.55 GB (about 148,100 tokens) 141 GB 129.72 GB H200 SXM $3.593 Llama 3.3 70B FP8, 57.05 GB (about 174,100 tokens) 180 GB 165.60 GB B200 $5.500 Llama 3.3 70B FP8, 92.93 GB (about 283,600 tokens) Cache room is usable memory minus the checkpoint size, and tokens are that room divided by the model's BF16 bytes per token. Prices checked November 14, 2026, on the Nodus pricing page . Precision also limits which hardware works. vLLM's FP8 documentation says FP8 compute runs on Ada Lovelace, Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, while Turing and Ampere cards such as the A100 and RTX A6000 run FP8 checkpoints as weight-only. If your number is larger than one GPU holds, split the model across GPUs with tensor parallelism: each GPU then holds its share of the weights and cache. How does Nodus pick a GPU that fits? You give Nodus the memory floor and it picks the hardware. Set resources.gpu.minMemory instead of a GPU type, and the Jobs guide says Nodus picks any accelerator with at least that much memory per GPU. Among the GPUs that qualify, the scheduler chooses by expected cost to finish. spec : resources : gpu : minMemory : 80Gi If you leave out minMemory , a nodus.dev/model annotation sets a floor from the model size: 24Gi for 7B and 8B models, 32Gi for 13B and 14B, 48Gi for 34B and 40B and 80Gi for 70B and 72B. That default covers the weights and a modest cache. Our worked example needs about 55 GB, so a busy 8B endpoint should set minMemory from the formula rather than rely on the 24Gi default. Before launching, nodus apply -f job.yaml --dry-run=server -o estimate shows the offering Nodus would use and the expected cost, without starting anything. Can you script the estimate in Python? This is the whole method in one function. We ran it on the worked example above and it prints the same numbers. def llm_vram_gb ( weights_gb , layers , kv_heads , head_dim , tokens , kv_bytes = 2 , gpu_util = 0.92 ) : """Serving estimate in decimal GB: (weights, KV cache, GPU memory needed).""" kv_gb = 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * kv_bytes * tokens / 1e9 return weights_gb , kv_gb , ( weights_gb + kv_gb ) / gpu_util # Llama 3.1 8B, BF16, 32 requests x 8,192 tokens w , kv , need = llm_vram_gb ( 16.06 , layers = 32 , kv_heads = 8 , head_dim = 128 , tokens = 32 * 8192 ) print ( f "weights {w:.2f} GB, KV {kv:.2f} GB, need {need:.2f} GB" ) # weights 16.06 GB, KV 34.36 GB, need 54.80 GB Pass kv_bytes=1 for an FP8 cache. For weights_gb , use the checkpoint size on Hugging Face, or parameters x the effective bytes from the weights section. What changes when you fine-tune instead of serve? Training multiplies the weight term, because gradients and optimizer state live next to every trainable parameter. Mixed-precision training with Adam takes about 16 bytes per parameter, so Llama 3.1 8B needs 128.5 GB before a single activation. LoRA and QLoRA freeze the base model and cut that to a fraction. The CUDA out-of-memory guide walks through each bucket and the fixes in order, and the 70B post prices full, LoRA and QLoRA fine-tuning at that size. FAQ How much VRAM do you need to run an LLM locally? An 8B model in 4-bit fits on a 24 GB card with room for long chats: Qwen3-8B AWQ is 6.10 GB, leaving 15.98 GB, about 108,000 tokens of cache. Even a 12 GB card can hold the weights, but then the cache limits how long a conversation can run. Are online LLM VRAM calculators accurate? They are as accurate as the key-value head count and the precision they assume. Check that a calculator reads num_key_value_heads rather than the query heads, and that its INT4 figure includes the 16-bit embeddings and scales. Does a longer context window use more VRAM if I do not fill it? With vLLM, the engine reserves its cache up front from the memory fraction, not from the context window. The maximum context length only matters because one request must fit in the cache, so a 131,072-token Llama 3.1 8B request needs 17.18 GB of cache by itself. Can Nodus tell me before launch which GPU memory floor it will use? Yes. nodus apply -f job.yaml --dry-run=server -o yaml shows the floor Nodus picked from your minMemory or model annotation, and the -o estimate form shows the offering and expected cost. Neither starts a machine. Does tensor parallelism split the KV cache too? Yes, each GPU stores the cache for its own key-value heads, so the per-GPU cache shrinks with the GPU count. With 8 key-value heads, as in every model above, that split stops helping past 8 GPUs, because engines then replicate heads instead of dividing them. Originally published on the Nodus blog .

title: Who actually arrived: telling a reader, a crawler, and your own robot apart in one event table
author: MapToSite
summary: You ship a small page. You add a counter. A week later the counter says thirteen visitors, and you start making decisions from it — this copy works, that aggregator sends traffic, the landing page is worth improving. Then you look at the rows and find that four of the thirteen were not people at all. Two were your own deploy check. One was a crawler. One was a link-preview bot from a chat app, fetching your title so a stranger could see a card. You did not lose the visitors; you never had them. The number was never a count of people. It was a count of requests, and requests are made by programs. This article is about the small event table that fixes that, the classification ladder that makes its numbers defensible, and the specific ways those numbers lie even after you build it properly. It is written for the case most solo builders are actually in: no analytics vendor, no consent banner, one table you control, and a need to answer "did anyone come, and did they do anything" without fooling yourself. A row is an observation, not a person Start with the honest description of the data. Each row records that something fetched a URL at a time, with a referrer it claimed, from an address your server saw, with a user agent it volunteered. Everything about a person is inference on top of that. So the table should hold what you can defend, and nothing that pretends to know more: column what it is what it must not become created_at server time of the request, stored in UTC a local time you have to re-derive later path the route that was fetched, normalised a full URL with query strings you cannot group event a small closed set: view , click , copy free text referrer exactly what the header said, blanks included a guessed source ip_hash salted hash of the client address the address itself meta device class, a probe marker, the raw user agent a place to stuff fifty columns is_internal 0/1 — is this our own traffic a deletion flag internal_reason why it was classified internal empty on internal rows Two of those deserve arguing. Do not store raw addresses. A salted hash is enough to deduplicate a session and useless for identifying a household, which is the correct trade for a page that wants no cookie banner. Rotate the salt on a schedule you choose, because a stable salt is a pseudonym that outlives its purpose. Do not delete your own traffic; flag it. Internal rows are the audit trail that your deploy, your check script and your monitoring all still work. Delete them and the next time the counter reads zero you cannot tell whether the page is fine or the instrumentation died. Keep the row, exclude it by is_internal = 0 in every query, and require a reason string so a later you can disagree with the classification. The ladder: classify in order, and name the remainder honestly The temptation is a single boolean, is_bot . That boolean will be wrong in both directions: it will mark a curious reader who pastes a link into a terminal as a robot, and it will let a headless browser through because it had no user agent at all. Use an ordered ladder instead, first match wins: Us. A path marker, a header, or an address we know is ours. Reason: probe , deploy-check , monitor . Declared crawler. User agent matches a known crawler family. Reason: ua:googlebot . Undeclared automation. No referrer, one event, no downstream event ever, user agent truncated or absent, or a burst at a machine cadence. Reason: shape:no-referrer-single . Link preview / unfurl. A fetch of the HTML with a HEAD-like pattern or a request seconds after a share, often from a datacenter address, often from an app's preview service. Reason: shape:unfurl . Unclassified. Everything else. And then the naming discipline that matters more than the ladder: the last bucket is "not identified as a robot" , not "human". Report it that way. A number labelled honestly is still useful; a number labelled wishfully gets built on. The reason strings are the part that pays off months later. When you reclassify, you reclassify by reason, not by guessing which rows were which: SELECT coalesce(nullif(internal_reason,''),'(none)') reason, is_internal, count(*) n, count(distinct ip_hash) ppl FROM traffic_events WHERE created_at >= ? GROUP BY reason, is_internal ORDER BY n DESC Your own traffic is the largest contaminant, and the easiest to fix Every deploy you open the page to see whether the stylesheet loaded. Every check script you will write over the next month (see the companion piece on schedules and checks) touches the same route. Left alone, that is a steady drip of "visitors" that scales with how much you work — which is precisely backwards, because the busiest weeks look like the most successful ones. Three fixes, in order of preference: Separate origin. Put the pre-deploy view on a staging host. Then production can only be reached by production traffic and your own probes, of which there are few. Mark the probe at the source. One header, checked once in the request handler, recorded as is_internal=1 with the reason. This is a two-line change and it survives every future script, because every future script copies the one you wrote today. Recognise by address. A fallback when you cannot touch the code path: the egress address of your own worker, recorded with a reason like ip:worker . This is the weakest option: shared egress means you may swallow someone else's traffic, and a changed egress silently stops working. The failure mode to plan against: an internal exclusion that quietly catches real people. That happens when the rule is broad — "user agent contains curl " — and someone genuinely arrives from a terminal. The reason string is what saves you: when the totals look wrong, sort by reason and read the rows. Crawlers announce themselves, and that is all the user agent is worth A user agent is self-reported and trivially forgeable, so it is evidence, never proof. What a crawler actually looks like in an event table is a shape, and the shape is more reliable than the string: no referrer, because the crawler was handed a URL rather than following a link on a page; a single event, because it does not click; a fetch of /robots.txt and a sitemap shortly before, if you log every path and not just your pages; a request pattern that repeats on a fixed interval across many URLs, which no reader does. Reverse DNS is not the answer either — it is slow, frequently absent, and still spoofable in the direction that matters. If you need proof, verify that a claimed crawler address belongs to the crawler's published ranges, and cache the result. Otherwise accept that you are estimating, and keep the reason string so the estimate is auditable. There is one more crawler class worth its own bucket because it confuses funnel math: the preview fetcher . When someone shares your link in a chat app, the app fetches the page to render a card. That request is a real request, sometimes from a real person's account, and it produces a view with no click, no scroll, and no second request. If your page's job is to get someone to press a button, a preview fetch is a false positive on the first funnel step, and it arrives exactly when you have shared the link somewhere — which is when you are most eager to read the numbers. Time: measure at both ends, and watermark by id Two habits make "nothing happened" a claim instead of a guess. Measure twice: at the start and the end of the work. A job that reads the table at 06:54 and reports "zero new" is making a statement about a window it never defined. Read again at 07:01, and now the statement is: from row 687 to row 687, over the interval between two timestamps. Nine quiet minutes. That is a fact, and it is falsifiable. This is not pedantry. Events land between runs. A visitor who arrives two minutes after one run's last read and before the next run's scheduled time is invisible to both the "no traffic" report and the "we had traffic" report, and you will spend an afternoon trying to explain why a channel appears to do nothing while the totals keep growing: run start: SELECT max(id) mx, count(*) n, max(created_at) last FROM events; ... work ... run end: SELECT max(id) mx, count(*) n, max(created_at) last FROM events; delta: n_end - n_start, and every row with id > start.mx Watermark by id, not by timestamp. WHERE created_at > last_seen skips rows that share a second with the watermark — and in a burst, several rows do. Ids from a monotonically increasing sequence give you an exact, tie-free boundary. If you do not have one, take the timestamp as a boundary and the max id at that timestamp. Store UTC; display local. One field, one timezone, converted at the edge. The alternative is a database whose meaning depends on which report you are reading, and a bug you will find at the worst possible hour. Rates from tiny numbers are fiction You will have days that look like this: thirteen view rows, two click rows. The arithmetic that leaps to mind is 15.4%, and it is worse than useless — it invites a decision about copy from a sample where one more click would move the number eight points. The rule I use: report counts until n is large enough to make a rate meaningful, and always name the denominator. "Two clicks from thirteen arrivals, over 24 hours, two of the arrivals on different days" is honest. "15% click-through" implies a stability the data does not have. The same caution applies to deduplication. Counting rows counts events; counting distinct ip_hash counts something like sessions. They answer different questions, and the gap between them is information: thirteen rows from thirteen hashes is thirteen separate arrivals; thirteen rows from three hashes is one enthusiast and a refresh button. Choose deliberately, and print both. The referrer is the cheapest attribution you have, and it is mostly blank The referrer header is the only free signal that says how someone arrived, and browsers strip it constantly: cross-origin navigation without a referrer policy, links opened from apps, and anything typed or pasted. So a blank referrer is not "direct traffic". It is "unknown", and labelling it "direct" in a report is how people conclude that their search traffic is worthless. What the referrer is good for is chains. If your link is listed on an aggregator page, and that page links to three of your routes, you will see a recognisable shape: path event referrer reading /guide view https://aggregator.example/ arrived from the listing /guide view blank arrived from a message, or the same person later /buy click https://aggregator.example/guide the listing's link, followed through And when a path has views but the next step in the funnel has never a single row from any referrer, that is a finding of its own — though not the finding you want. It can be a copy problem (nobody wanted to press it) or an instrumentation problem (the button's event never fires). The table alone cannot tell you which; you find out by being one of the arrivals and checking that your own click produced a row. That check — do my own events appear, and with the shape I expect — is worth running after every change to the page. An event table nobody has verified against their own behaviour is a table of wishes. What the table cannot tell you, and what to add instead Three things people expect an event table to answer, which it does not: Whether someone converted. A view and a click in your table are both things that happened on your site. Whatever happens after the click happens in someone else's system — a storefront, an app store, an invite screen. If you cannot observe it, do not report it. Report the click through to your boundary and stop. Whether a page was read . A pageview is a fetch. Time-on-page requires a second event (a visibility change, a scroll), and even then it measures the tab, not the attention. Whether a channel "works". Channels produce arrivals, arrivals produce clicks, clicks produce whatever happens downstream. A channel with arrivals and no clicks is a messaging problem; a channel with no arrivals is a distribution problem. One number cannot distinguish them, and the most common analytic mistake in a solo project is adding distribution effort to a conversion problem. The one addition that pays for itself: the same classification on the downstream event as on the arrival , so the funnel's steps are computed over the same population. If arrivals exclude robots and clicks do not, your conversion rate silently includes robots clicking. Retention: keep raw rows until you know the questions Aggregating early feels tidy and is a one-way door. Daily rollups answer "how many on Tuesday" and cannot answer "did the arrivals from that listing click", which is the question you will actually have in three weeks. Keep raw rows long enough to cover the questions you can currently imagine asking — a few months for a personal project — then roll up to daily counts by path, event, referrer class, plus the distinct-person count. Aggregate by reason as well as flag, so a later reclassification does not require the raw rows you just deleted. The checklist Every row records UTC time, normalised path, one of a small set of events, the raw referrer including blanks, a salted address hash, a device class and a probe marker. Internal traffic is flagged with a reason, never deleted. Classification is an ordered ladder ending in "not identified as a robot", not in a boolean named is_bot . User agent is a hint; the shape (no referrer, one event, no click, machine cadence) is the evidence. Preview fetchers are their own bucket, because they inflate the first funnel step at exactly the moment you are watching. The table is read at both the start and the end of any job that reports on it, and the report names the window. Watermarks are ids, not timestamps. Rates wait for n; until then, counts with a denominator. A blank referrer is "unknown". Downstream events carry the same classification as arrivals. Someone has personally verified that their own click produces the expected row. None of this makes the table correct. It makes it auditable — which is the only property that matters, because the moment you trust a number you cannot explain, you have stopped measuring and started guessing with extra steps. Disclosure: I build and write about small automation tools, and I run an English guide for an AI assistant app whose invite system I use as a working example of these ideas: Pickle invite code SY3LC2 — how to enter it and the invite link pickle.com/i/RDKXK77G9ZRT . If someone joins through that link, I receive in-app usage credit; it costs the person joining nothing. Nothing in the article depends on that product, and the analytics design described is generic.

title: Validar CPF e CNPJ em JavaScript: o módulo 11 explicado (e o CNPJ alfanumérico de 2026)
author: Doit Follow
summary: Se você já montou um formulário de cadastro no Brasil, já precisou validar CPF e CNPJ no front-end antes de enviar os dados. A boa notícia: a regra é pública, determinística e cabe em poucas linhas de JavaScript — os dois documentos usam o módulo 11 para gerar os dígitos verificadores. Neste artigo eu explico a conta passo a passo, mostro a implementação e ainda cubro a mudança que chega em 2026: o CNPJ alfanumérico . CPF: 9 dígitos + 2 verificadores Um CPF tem 11 dígitos. Os 9 primeiros são a base; os 2 últimos são calculados assim: Primeiro verificador: multiplique os 9 dígitos pelos pesos 10, 9, 8 … 2 , some tudo e divida por 11. Se o resto for 0 ou 1, o dígito é 0 ; senão, é 11 − resto . Segundo verificador: repita com os 10 primeiros dígitos (incluindo o verificador que você acabou de calcular) e os pesos 11, 10, 9 … 2 , com a mesma regra. Exemplo real, com o CPF fictício 111.444.777-35 : 1×10 + 1×9 + 1×8 + 4×7 + 4×6 + 4×5 + 7×4 + 7×3 + 7×2 = 162 → 162 ÷ 11 tem resto 8 → dígito = 11 − 8 = 3 ✓ 1×11 + 1×10 + 1×9 + 4×8 + 4×7 + 4×6 + 7×5 + 7×4 + 7×3 + 3×2 = 204 → resto 6 → dígito = 11 − 6 = 5 ✓ Os dois dígitos conferem: o CPF é válido pela regra matemática . function validarCPF ( cpf ) { const d = cpf . replace ( / \ D / g , "" ) ; if ( d . length !== 11 || /^ ( \ d ) \ 1 { 10 } $ / . test ( d ) ) return false ; const digito = ( base , pesoInicial ) => { let soma = 0 ; for ( let i = 0 ; i < base . length ; i ++ ) soma += Number ( base [ i ] ) * ( pesoInicial - i ) ; const resto = ( soma * 10 ) % 11 ; return resto === 10 || resto === 11 ? 0 : resto ; } ; return digito ( d . slice ( 0 , 9 ) , 10 ) === Number ( d [ 9 ] ) && digito ( d . slice ( 0 , 10 ) , 11 ) === Number ( d [ 10 ] ) ; } validarCPF ( "111.444.777-35" ) ; // true validarCPF ( "111.444.777-34" ) ; // false — trocou um dígito, quebrou a conta validarCPF ( "111.111.111-11" ) ; // false — sequência repetida (ver abaixo) A pegadinha: dígitos repetidos "passam" na conta Sequências como 111.111.111-11 e 000.000.000-00 satisfazem o módulo 11, mas nenhum CPF real é assim — por isso a validação precisa rejeitá-las explicitamente (é o regex /^(\d)\1{10}$/ no código acima). Esquecer esse passo é o erro mais comum que vejo em implementações por aí. CNPJ: os pesos "andam" de 2 a 9 O CNPJ tem 14 dígitos (12 de base + 2 verificadores). A lógica é a mesma, mas os pesos não descem de 13 e 12: eles ciclam de 2 a 9 , da direita para a esquerda. Para o primeiro verificador, os pesos sobre os 12 dígitos são 5 4 3 2 9 8 7 6 5 4 3 2 ; para o segundo, sobre 13 dígitos, 6 5 4 3 2 9 8 7 6 5 4 3 2 . A regra do resto muda um pouco: se soma % 11 < 2 , o dígito é 0; senão, é 11 − (soma % 11) . 2026: o CNPJ alfanumérico A partir de julho de 2026 , novos CNPJs poderão ter letras nas 12 primeiras posições (os 2 verificadores continuam numéricos). A validação quase não muda: cada caractere vira um valor numérico pelo código ASCII menos 48 — dígitos valem o próprio valor ( 0 – 9 ) e letras valem de 17 em diante ( A = 65 − 48 = 17, B = 18, …). Depois disso, é o mesmo módulo 11 com os mesmos pesos. Exemplo calculado com essa regra: a base 12.ABC.345/01DE vira os valores 1, 2, 17, 18, 19, 3, 4, 5, 0, 1, 20, 21 , e os verificadores resultantes são 3 e 5 — ou seja, o CNPJ completo 12.ABC.345/01DE-35 é válido pela nova regra. Se o seu sistema valida CNPJ, vale adaptar o código agora: basta trocar o Number(d[i]) por d.charCodeAt(i) - 48 e parar de rejeitar letras na máscara. Validar não é consultar Um último cuidado, que confunde muita gente: passar no módulo 11 só prova que o número respeita a regra matemática . Não prova que o documento existe, pertence a alguém ou está regular na Receita Federal — isso só a consulta oficial confirma. Validação client-side serve para pegar erro de digitação cedo e melhorar a experiência do formulário; situação cadastral é outra camada. Quer testar sem escrever código? No JeitoBR — um site de ferramentas gratuitas que eu mantenho — o validador de CPF e o validador e consulta de CNPJ rodam 100% no navegador, com a mesma lógica deste artigo (o de CNPJ já consulta a situação na Receita). Se você encontrar algum caso em que a sua implementação discorda da minha, me conta nos comentários — adoro um edge case novo.

title: You Type a URL and Hit Enter. What Actually Happens Behind the Scenes?
author: Henrry George
summary:
Have you ever wondered what happens between typing https://example.com into your browser and seeing the website appear on your screen? It feels almost instant. You enter a URL, press Enter, wait a moment, and the webpage appears. You can click buttons, open menus, watch videos, and interact with different elements. But behind that simple action, several technologies work together. DNS finds the server. Network protocols establish communication. HTTPS protects the connection. The server processes your request and sends a response. Finally, the browser turns HTML, CSS, and JavaScript into the webpage you see. Understanding this process is one of the most useful things a web developer can learn. Whether you're building websites, developing APIs, working with frontend frameworks, or learning backend development, knowing what happens behind the scenes helps you understand how the web actually works. Let's follow a single request from the moment you press Enter. 1. The Browser First Understands the URL Imagine you enter this address: https://www.example.com/products?id=25 Before contacting a server, the browser interprets the URL. A URL contains several parts: Component Example Purpose Protocol https Defines how communication is secured Hostname www.example.com Identifies the destination Path /products Identifies the requested resource Query string ?id=25 Provides additional parameters The browser uses this information to determine where the request should go and how it should communicate. For example, HTTPS normally uses port 443, while HTTP normally uses port 80. If the URL contains a fragment such as #reviews , that fragment is generally handled by the browser and isn't sent as part of the HTTP request. But there's still one important problem. The browser knows the website's domain name, but it needs an IP address to communicate with the destination. That's where DNS comes in. 2. DNS Finds the Website's IP Address DNS stands for Domain Name System. Think of it as the internet's address directory. Humans remember names like: google.com github.com example.com Computers use IP addresses to route network traffic. When your browser needs to reach a domain, it uses DNS resolution to discover the appropriate IP address. A simplified DNS lookup works like this: The browser or operating system checks available DNS caches. If the answer isn't cached, a DNS resolver is contacted. The resolver may query other DNS servers to find the required record. The resolver returns the result, such as an A or AAAA record. The browser can use the returned address to establish a connection. For example, an IPv4 DNS record might look like this: example.com → 93.184.216.34 This is an illustrative example of DNS mapping, not a guarantee that the address will remain the same. You can try looking up a domain yourself: nslookup example.com Or use: dig example.com These commands help developers understand how domain names resolve to IP addresses. Why does DNS matter? Without DNS, people would need to remember IP addresses instead of convenient domain names. It also plays an important role in website infrastructure, including load balancing, content delivery networks, and domain management. 3. The Browser Establishes a Connection Now the browser knows where it needs to send the request. The next step is establishing communication. For HTTPS websites, this typically involves a secure connection using TLS. There are two common transport approaches worth understanding. TCP Traditional HTTPS connections commonly use TCP. TCP establishes a connection between the client and server through a process known as the three-way handshake. The process involves: SYN: The client requests a connection. SYN-ACK: The server acknowledges the request. ACK: The client confirms the connection. After this process, both sides can exchange data over the established TCP connection. QUIC Modern HTTP/3 uses QUIC, which runs over UDP rather than TCP. QUIC integrates transport security using TLS 1.3 and provides connection establishment and stream handling designed for modern internet communication. This distinction matters because HTTP/3 doesn't use the traditional TCP three-way handshake. What About TLS? For a secure HTTPS connection, TLS helps protect communication between the browser and the server. During a TLS handshake, the client and server negotiate security parameters, authenticate the server using its certificate, and establish shared encryption keys. This helps protect sensitive information from being read or modified while traveling across the network. For example, when you submit login credentials through HTTPS, the connection encrypts the communication between your browser and the server. You can learn more through MDN's TLS documentation. 4. The Browser Sends an HTTP Request Once the necessary connection is ready, the browser can send an HTTP request. HTTP stands for Hypertext Transfer Protocol. It defines how clients and servers exchange information. A simplified HTTP request might look like this: GET /products?id = 25 HTTP / 1.1 Host : www . example . com Accept : text / html User - Agent : ExampleBrowser This request communicates several things: GET is the HTTP method. /products?id=25 identifies the requested resource. Host identifies the requested hostname. Accept indicates the content types the client can accept. User-Agent identifies the requesting software. There are several HTTP methods developers commonly use: Method Common Purpose GET Retrieve information POST Submit data PUT Replace a resource PATCH Partially update a resource DELETE Delete a resource For example, when a user opens a product page, the browser might send a GET request. When a user submits a registration form, the application might send a POST request containing the submitted information. You can inspect HTTP requests yourself using Chrome DevTools. Open a website, press F12, select the Network tab, and reload the page. You'll see requests, response codes, headers, resource sizes, and timing information. This is one of the most useful debugging techniques for web developers. 5. The Request Reaches a Server After leaving the browser, the request travels through the network infrastructure toward its destination. Depending on the website's architecture, it may pass through: Routers and network gateways. A content delivery network (CDN). A reverse proxy. A load balancer. A web server. An application server. Not every website uses all these components. For example, a simple static website might be served directly from a CDN without running application code for every request. A dynamic application may require backend processing. Imagine a user visiting an ecommerce product page. The backend might need to: Identify the requested product. Retrieve product information from a database. Check inventory. Load relevant images or metadata. Generate an appropriate response. A simplified Node.js example might look like this: import express from "express" ; const app = express ( ) ; app . get ( "/products/:id" , async ( req , res ) => { const productId = req . params . id ; // Example data for demonstration const product = { id : productId , name : "Wireless Headphones" , price : 79 } ; res . json ( product ) ; } ) ; app . listen ( 3000 , ( ) => { console . log ( "Server running on port 3000" ) ; } ) ; When a client requests /products/25 , the server processes the route and returns a JSON response. Real applications would usually retrieve product information from a database and include validation, error handling, and appropriate security checks. 6. The Server Sends an HTTP Response After processing the request, the server sends an HTTP response. A simplified response might look like this: HTTP / 1.1 200 OK Content - Type : application / json { "id" : "25" , "name" : "Wireless Headphones" , "price" : 79 } The response contains a status code, headers, and sometimes a response body. Here are some HTTP status codes developers should recognize: Status Meaning 200 OK 201 Created 301 Moved Permanently 302 Found 400 Bad Request 401 Unauthorized 403 Forbidden 404 Not Found 500 Internal Server Error 503 Service Unavailable These codes help the browser and other clients understand what happened during a request. For example: A 200 response generally means the request succeeded. A 404 response means the requested resource wasn't found. A 500 response indicates an internal server error. An important detail: a successful HTTP response doesn't necessarily mean the application operation was successful in a business sense. Developers still need to inspect the response body and application-level errors. 7. The Browser Starts Building the Webpage This is where things become particularly interesting for frontend developers. The browser receives HTML and begins processing it. It doesn't simply display the HTML as a finished document. Instead, it parses the markup and builds an internal representation called the DOM (Document Object Model). Consider this HTML: My Website

Hello, Developers!

Welcome to my website.

The browser parses this document and creates a tree-like structure. Conceptually, the DOM looks something like this: Document └── html ├── head │ └── title └── body ├── h1 └── p The DOM represents the structure and content of the page. JavaScript can interact with it through browser APIs. For example: const heading = document . querySelector ( "h1" ) ; heading . textContent = "Welcome to Web Development!" ; This changes the heading's text without requiring a completely new HTML document. 8. CSS Builds the Visual Appearance HTML provides structure, but CSS controls how the page looks. When the browser processes CSS, it builds another internal representation called the CSSOM (CSS Object Model). For example: body { font-family : Arial , sans-serif ; background : #f5f5f5 ; } h1 { color : #2563eb ; font-size : 32px ; } The browser uses CSS rules to determine how HTML elements should appear. It then combines the DOM and CSSOM information to construct a render tree. The render tree contains the visible elements and their computed styles. This is an important part of the browser's critical rendering path. 9. Layout, Paint, and Compositing Turn Everything Into Pixels Once the browser has the information needed to render the page, it performs several operations. Layout The browser calculates the size and position of visible elements. For example: Where should the navigation bar appear? How wide should the main content be? Where should an image be positioned? How much space should exist between sections? Paint The browser determines how individual elements should be visually drawn. This includes text, backgrounds, borders, shadows, and other visual details. Compositing The browser combines different visual layers into the final image displayed on the screen. Some content may be composited using the GPU, depending on the browser and rendering requirements. The overall process can be simplified as: HTML ↓ DOM CSS ↓ CSSOM DOM + CSSOM ↓ Render Tree ↓ Layout ↓ Paint ↓ Compositing ↓ Pixels on Screen This is how the browser transforms code into the visual webpage you interact with. 10. The Browser Continues Loading Other Resources Receiving the initial HTML doesn't mean the entire website has finished loading. The HTML may reference additional resources: Stylesheets. JavaScript files. Images. Fonts. Videos. API endpoints. The browser discovers these resources and requests them when necessary. For example: The browser needs to download and process the relevant resources to complete the page experience. This is also why developers need to understand resource loading priorities. A stylesheet can block rendering while it is being processed. A traditional synchronous script can block HTML parsing. Using defer , appropriate loading priorities, and optimized resource delivery can help improve the initial experience. However, not every resource must finish loading before the browser can show useful content. The browser can progressively process and render a page as resources become available. 11. What Happens When You Click Something? The process doesn't stop after the initial page appears. When you click a button, JavaScript may respond to the interaction. For example: const button = document . querySelector ( "#load-products" ) ; button . addEventListener ( "click" , async ( ) => { const response = await fetch ( "/api/products" ) ; if ( ! response . ok ) { throw new Error ( "Unable to load products" ) ; } const products = await response . json ( ) ; console . log ( products ) ; } ) ; Here is what happens: The user clicks the button. JavaScript handles the click event. The browser sends a request using fetch() . The server processes the request. The server returns a response. JavaScript processes the returned JSON. The application can then update the interface using the received data. This is how many modern websites provide interactive experiences without reloading the entire document. The Entire Journey in One Diagram Let's put everything together. User Enters a URL | v Browser Parses URL | v DNS Resolves Domain | v Connection Established (TCP or QUIC) | v TLS Security (HTTPS) | v HTTP Request Sent | v Server / CDN Processes Request | v HTTP Response Returned | v Browser Receives HTML | v DOM + CSSOM Created | v Render Tree Constructed | v Layout -> Paint -> Composite | v Webpage Appears | v User Interacts With Website This is a simplified overview. Real browsers and network architectures can perform several of these operations concurrently, reuse existing connections, serve cached resources, and follow different paths depending on the protocol and website infrastructure. Why Understanding This Process Matters for Developers You might wonder why a frontend developer needs to understand DNS or TLS. The answer is simple: websites don't operate in isolated layers. A frontend problem might actually originate from the backend. A slow page might be caused by DNS resolution, a delayed server response, a large JavaScript bundle, or a render-blocking stylesheet. Understanding the complete request lifecycle helps developers investigate problems more effectively. For example: Problem Where to Investigate Domain doesn't resolve DNS configuration Secure connection fails TLS certificate and configuration Server returns 404 URL, routing, and server configuration Server returns 500 Backend application and logs API response is slow Network, server, and database Page appears without styling CSS loading and processing Button doesn't respond JavaScript and event handling Instead of randomly changing code, you can investigate the layer where the problem actually occurs. Understanding these concepts is also valuable when planning real-world digital projects. From website architecture and user experience to frontend development and technical implementation, every decision contributes to the final product. At The Creative Unit , we explore creative digital solutions, website design, and development that help businesses build a stronger online presence. Tools Every Web Developer Should Know If you want to understand what happens when a browser loads a website, these tools are worth exploring. 1. Chrome DevTools The Network tab lets you inspect requests, responses, headers, status codes, and loading times. Chrome DevTools Network Documentation 2. DNS Lookup Tools Commands such as nslookup and dig help investigate domain resolution. 3. cURL You can make HTTP requests directly from your terminal. curl -I https://example.com This displays response headers and helps you inspect server responses. 4. Wireshark Wireshark allows developers and network engineers to inspect network traffic and investigate communication problems. Visit Wireshark 5. MDN Web Docs MDN provides detailed explanations of HTTP, DNS, browser rendering, JavaScript, and other web technologies. Explore MDN Web Docs Final Thoughts The next time you type a URL and press Enter, remember that a lot more is happening than simply opening a webpage. Your browser interprets the URL, resolves the domain, establishes communication, sends an HTTP request, receives a response, processes HTML and CSS, executes JavaScript, and renders the result on your screen. Each stage plays an important role in making the modern web work. Understanding these fundamentals doesn't just help you become a better frontend developer. It also gives you a stronger foundation for backend development, API integration, debugging, security, and performance optimization. The web may feel instant to users, but behind every click is a fascinating chain of engineering decisions. Let's Discuss Before reading this article, did you know that your browser builds the DOM and CSSOM before constructing the render tree? Which part of this process do you find most interesting: DNS, HTTP communication, server-side processing, or browser rendering? Share your thoughts in the comments!
