title: The tampered Claude Code extension in Cursor's marketplace: what teams should check
author: Momin Aziz
summary: Originally published at ReclaimLLM . Cursor's notice on tampered Anthropic.claude-code 2.1.312 and 2.1.313: who was exposed, how to check a machine, and extension controls to add. The tampered Claude Code extension in Cursor's marketplace: what teams should check Updated November 14, 2026. On October 29, 2026, tampered copies of Anthropic's Claude Code extension were served from Cursor's VS Code extension marketplace for about 11 hours. Cursor's security notice provides indicators of compromise and cleanup scripts; its fuller incident update is dated November 13. This post summarizes what the official sources say, how a team can check its machines, and which extension controls to add. Everything about the malware comes from Cursor's notice and two independent analyses. Where the sources do not say something, we do not guess. What happened Affected artifact. Anthropic.claude-code versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 for Windows and macOS , installed or updated from the Cursor VS Code Extension Marketplace ( Cursor security notice ). Exposure window. About 2:27 a.m. to 1:35 p.m. Pacific Time on October 29, 2026 (about 5:27 a.m. to 4:35 p.m. in Toronto) ( Cursor security notice ). Who published it. Not Anthropic. Cursor's update says an attacker used a credential stolen from Cursor's internal systems to place the tampered copies directly on the cache that serves Cursor's extension marketplace. Cursor says this was not a vulnerability in Anthropic's product, and that Open VSX, the marketplace source, never had the malware ( Cursor incident update ). Microsoft reports that the malicious packages were never published on the Visual Studio Marketplace or in the npm package @anthropic-ai/claude-code ( Microsoft Security Blog ). StepSecurity reports that Anthropic confirmed 2.1.313 was never published on any official channel and skipped to 2.1.314 to avoid confusion ( StepSecurity ). How many people. Cursor says at most 5,000 users who requested specific cached versions on October 29 potentially received the malicious build, and that it contacted affected customers directly ( Cursor incident update ). How it started. Cursor's update traces the attack to an access key Cursor had issued to Fireworks, an inference vendor. The key was exposed at Fireworks, and the attacker used it to copy data from a storage bucket Cursor shared with Fireworks. That data included some credentials, which the attacker used to reach other Cursor systems ( Cursor incident update ; Fireworks security bulletins ). What was not affected, according to Cursor: other extensions in the marketplace, plugins from the Cursor Marketplace, the Cursor app and its official updates, customer code repositories, and prompts and code of users in Privacy Mode ( Cursor incident update ). What the malicious code did Cursor's notice says the tampered extension: Collected host and user details: hostname, username, OS, architecture, home directory path, environment variable names, working directories, configured Git email and public IP. Tried to add an attacker-controlled SSH key (comment svc-telemetry ) to authorized_keys , enable the local SSH service, and open a reverse SSH tunnel. Tried to persist through a LaunchAgent on macOS, or a scheduled task with a Startup-folder fallback on Windows. Cursor also says that turning on the SSH service needs admin rights, which the extension does not have on most macOS and Windows hosts, so on those hosts the tunnel step failed. But the extension still added the key, installed persistence and sent host details. The attacker's server has been taken offline ( Cursor security notice ). Microsoft's analysis adds two useful details. The loader sends environment variable names, not values. And the code runs when the extension module loads, so no Claude conversation is needed ( Microsoft Security Blog ). StepSecurity's analysis agrees that loading the module is enough ( StepSecurity ). Step 1: find out if any machine was exposed A version number alone does not prove compromise. StepSecurity notes that the 2.1.312 build on Open VSX is a different, clean file. What matters is the source (Cursor's marketplace), the platform (macOS or Windows) and the time (the October 29 window). List exposed machines. Use your endpoint or extension-installation telemetry to find Cursor installs that installed or auto-updated Anthropic.claude-code to 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 during the window. Check whether Cursor or your team admins received a notice from Cursor. Check each candidate machine for the SSH key. Cursor's notice gives a one-line check for macOS and a PowerShell check for Windows. Both look for svc-telemetry in the authorized keys files. Copy the commands from the notice, not from a third-party page. Hunt for the published indicators. A missing SSH marker alone does not rule out exposure; correlate installation records, process activity and persistence artifacts. The notice lists file hashes, the attacker IP, persistence file paths, the scheduled task name and the SSH command line. Microsoft publishes Defender hunting queries for the same indicators. Step 2: investigate and clean up affected machines Cursor's notice gives these steps for affected hosts ( Cursor security notice ): Isolate hosts that show signs of payload execution or backdoor installation. Remove the unauthorized SSH key, persistence and running tunnel processes. Cursor provides remediate-macos.sh (run as the affected user, not root) and remediate-windows.ps1 (run as Administrator). Assess whether the host should be rebuilt. Do not rely on uninstalling the extension. The payload drops standalone scripts outside the extension folder that keep running. Rotate credentials and sessions reachable from affected hosts, from a trusted system. Cursor says the limited environment-variable collection does not rule out later credential access over the backdoor. Microsoft adds: preserve evidence (the extension package, modified SSH files, scripts and startup entries) before cleanup, and keep unrelated SSH keys and legitimate remote-development settings ( Microsoft Security Blog ). Questions go to security@cursor.com , the contact both Cursor posts give. Step 3: add extension controls for next time Users in the Cursor forum asked whether they can trust plugin updates ( t/176923 ). Trust is a policy question. These controls reduce how much you depend on it. Allow only approved publishers. Cursor's security-hardening guide lists Allowed Extensions, an allowlist of trusted publishers. Note that the tampered copy here used Anthropic's real extension ID, so a publisher allowlist alone would not have stopped it ( Cursor security hardening ). Set an install cooldown. The same guide describes an extension install cooldown that defers installs and updates until a version has been public for a set number of hours, enforced fleet-wide, "to blunt short-lived malicious uploads". Microsoft recommends the same control. This exposure lasted about 11 hours, so the cooldown length matters. Turn on signature verification where available. Cursor's guide lists it as an optional part of the cooldown setting. Know where each extension came from. Record the marketplace source for your editor fleet. A version number is not enough to tell a clean build from a tampered one. Keep extension and MCP reviews separate. An editor extension, a plugin and an MCP server are different install paths with different controls. Our MCP security guide covers MCP servers. Limit what a compromised editor can reach. Short-lived credentials, no production secrets in shell environment variables, and SSH server disabled on laptops that do not need it all reduce the damage of any malicious extension. Cursor documents these controls in its enterprise hardening guidance. Check the linked configuration pages for your client version and deployment method; do not assume every plan supports the same fleet-wide enforcement. Where ReclaimLLM fits Use endpoint and extension-installation telemetry to investigate this incident. A captured AI session is not evidence that an extension was installed, and this article makes no claim that ReclaimLLM detected or blocked the tampered package. What it does: it captures AI coding sessions from Cursor, Claude Code, Copilot, Codex and Antigravity through hooks, and makes them searchable. After an incident like this, that record can help answer a narrower question: during the exposure window, which sensitive values appeared in the captured agent sessions on an affected machine. That is supplementary evidence: it cannot establish every credential the compromised host could access or narrow the vendor's rotation guidance. Detection of secrets and external egress in captured sessions runs on an hourly or daily sweep and raises alerts; it does not block. For the broader agent setup, see our Claude Code security guide . FAQ Was Anthropic hacked? Cursor says no: Anthropic did not publish the tampered copy, and it was not a vulnerability in Anthropic's product ( Cursor incident update ). Microsoft says Anthropic confirmed its systems were not compromised. I use Claude Code in VS Code, not Cursor. Am I affected? According to Cursor, Microsoft and StepSecurity, the tampered builds were only served from Cursor's marketplace. The Visual Studio Marketplace, Open VSX and the npm package were not affected. Is Linux affected? Cursor's notice names Windows and macOS builds. The indicator list also includes Linux file paths for the persistence scripts. Those artifacts do not establish that a malicious Linux package was distributed. If your Linux telemetry shows matching indicators, investigate them under your incident-response process. Does uninstalling the extension fix it? Not by itself. The payload installs scripts outside the extension folder. Follow Cursor's cleanup steps. Review your Cursor extension security . Read the original article at ReclaimLLM .

title: Which Model Should You Use? Frontier, Hosted or Local? It Depends.
author: xbill
summary: This article provides a roadmap for choosing where to run a model: on your own machine, through a hosted API, on Cloud Run, or on an accelerator you rent. Every figure comes from a measured run in gemma4-dev, which serves Gemma 4 on more than a hundred hardware and engine combinations and now carries five Gemini API models as sibling rigs. https://github.com/xbill9/gemma4-dev The New Gemini Models in One Table Gemini 4 Hydrogen, Carbon and Argon arrived on the Gemini API next to 3.5 Flash-Lite, 3.8 Flash and Gemma 4. On 2026-11-14 all seven ran through the same Gemini API endpoint, started together, with the same GSM8K (1,319 math word problems) and BFCL simple (400 function calls) questions and scoring, with thinking set as low as each model accepts: Model GSM8K BFCL simple Cost, both tasks Output price, per 1M tokens GSM8K median per request Gemma 4 31B 0.9735 🥇 0.9675 🥇 free tier free tier only 8.96 s Gemma 4 26B 0.9742 0.9575 🥇 free tier free tier only 8.16 s Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite 0.9629 0.9350 $0.92 $2.50 🥇 1.10 s Gemini 3.8 Flash 0.9788 0.9400 $1.81 $3.75 3.79 s Gemini 4 Hydrogen 0.9803 0.9550 $5.02 $7.50 🥈 2.84 s Gemini 4 Carbon 0.9803 0.9600 $4.02 $10.00 7.34 s Gemini 4 Argon 🥇 0.9841 🥇 0.9675 $3.46 $10.00 7.63 s Hydrogen, Carbon and Argon are ahead of Gemma 4 31B on GSM8K, with the 95% range of the difference above zero, and level with it on BFCL. Output prices include thinking tokens, and thinking decides the bill. On Hydrogen and 3.8 Flash it cannot be turned off: Hydrogen has the lowest Gemini 4 price, thought on every problem at its lowest setting, and cost the most. It is also the fastest Gemini 4 model, about 2.7 times quicker per problem than Argon. The times come from all seven sharing one connection at once. Carbon and Argon double in price on 2026-12-01. The method is in the companion article, Gemini 4 Hydrogen, Carbon and Argon Against Gemma 4 . The Options Four ways to run a model, each measured in this repo: Local: a GPU or CPU you own. Measured on an RTX 3050 OEM (8 GB desktop card), a GTX 1650 Ti (4 GB laptop card) and an Intel i7-10750H laptop CPU. Hosted API: someone else's server, reached with a key. Measured on the Gemini API (the five Gemini models) and AMD Token Lab (Gemma 4 31B, free with the AMD AI Developer Program). Cloud Run: Google's serverless containers with one NVIDIA L4, serving Gemma 4 E2B on vLLM. Your own accelerator: a rented machine you start and stop. Measured on a TPU v5e (one chip and four), an EC2 G6 with one L4, and an AMD MI300X on DigitalOcean. Option 1 — Local The RTX 3050 serves Gemma 4 E2B on six engines. One request at a time without a drafter they run from 61.9 tok/s (LiteRT-LM) to 121.1 tok/s (vLLM); with Google's speculative-decoding drafter vLLM reaches 230.5 tok/s. Under load, with 64 requests at once of 128 tokens in and 512 out, SGLang delivers 1,711.3 tok/s in total and vLLM 1,651.2. The same card holds the larger models one request at a time: 12B at 56.4 tok/s with its drafter, 26B A4B at 40.6 tok/s on code with its experts in system RAM, and 31B at 4.0 tok/s with two thirds of it on the CPU. Quality rises with size: GSM8K 0.9014 (E2B), 0.9629 (12B), 0.9735 (31B). The 1650 Ti laptop card decodes E2B at 73.75 tok/s for one request and peaks at 164 tok/s through its server at 16 requests. The laptop CPU decodes 16.71 to 18.86 tok/s. Setup: llama.cpp is ready 4 s after start, vLLM 48 s. vLLM's first start compiles for about 3.5 minutes. The hardware is already paid for, and nothing is billed per hour. Option 2 — Hosted API Gemini API. A key and an HTTP call. The Gemini models and Gemma 4 26B and 31B answer the OpenAI chat format at /v1beta/openai/chat/completions . Estimated from the token counts returned and list prices, a full 1,319-problem GSM8K run cost $0.87 on Flash-Lite, $1.66 on 3.8 Flash, $3.15 on Argon, $3.70 on Carbon and $4.51 on Hydrogen. Gemma 4 is on the free tier only, with paid use not available, and its free-tier rate limit answered three requests in the GSM8K and BFCL runs with HTTP 429 after every retry. AMD Token Lab. Gemma 4 31B on an SGLang router on AMD GPUs, free with the AMD AI Developer Program: 10 points for 30 days, with Gemma 4 31B at 0.035 points per million input tokens and 0.07 per million output. One request at a time decoded at 2.0 to 7.6 tok/s on the shared service, with up to 5 s before the first token. The limit is 128 requests at once across all users; over that, the reply is HTTP 429. Option 3 — Cloud Run One L4 GPU in us-east4 with 8 vCPU and 32 GiB, Gemma 4 E2B on vLLM. Output rose with concurrency to 188.46 tok/s at 4 requests and stayed there at 8 (189.53), because the service was deployed with --concurrency=4 ; more users means more instances. The same L4 on EC2 reached 360.17 tok/s at 8. At list price the instance costs $1.4209 an hour, which works out to $7.95 per million output tokens at one request and $2.08 at eight. Cloud Run scales to zero by default, so an idle service costs nothing and the next request waits for a cold GPU start; the startup check waits 180 s before its first look. The weights load from Cloud Storage. Option 4 — Your Own Accelerator TPU v5e, one chip. Gemma 4 E2B on vLLM: 143.9 tok/s for one request, 1,689.1 tok/s at 64 requests (128 in, 512 out), GSM8K 0.9007 and BFCL 0.920. Flex-start costs $0.60 per chip-hour, about $0.089 per million output tokens at full batching and $1.31 at one request. Capacity came within two to five minutes in us-west4-a , and the engine took 12.6 to 14.1 minutes to start on most rigs, most of it compiling (27.2 on one). TPU v5e, four chips. E2B as four one-chip engines reaches 7,788 tok/s at 64 requests and 14,189 at 256. The 12B fits with 122,624 tokens of context cache, against 9,728 on one chip. EC2 G6, one L4. vLLM at 132.8 to 140.4 tok/s for one request and 3,715.7 tok/s at 64; with the drafter, 4,516.3. A spot g6.2xlarge measured on an older vLLM cost $0.9412 an hour, $0.73 per million output tokens at eight requests. AMD MI300X. 192 GB on one card: E2B at 340.4 tok/s for one request and 10,293.6 tok/s at 64 (128 tokens of context). $1.99 an hour, billed while powered off too: $0.054 per million output tokens at 64 clients and $1.624 for a single stream. 🔎 Tip: Price Per Hour Becomes Price Per Token Only Under Load Every rented option above has two prices per million tokens, one at a single request and one at full batching: Cloud Run $7.95 and $2.08, TPU v5e $1.31 and $0.089, MI300X $1.624 and $0.054. A machine that serves one user at a time costs about what a hosted API charges, or more. A per-token API charges the same at any load. Compare and Contrast Local 3050 Gemini API Token Lab Cloud Run L4 TPU v5e-1 MI300X Users at once 64 measured 8 measured 128 shared 4 per instance 64 measured 64 measured Most output, tok/s 1,711.3 not measured not measured 189.53 1,689.1 🥇 10,293.6 One request, tok/s 230.5 not measured 2.0–7.6 49.63 143.9 340.4 Cost 🥇 card you own per token 🥇 free $1.4209/hr $0.60/hr $1.99/hr Best GSM8K 0.9735 (31B) 🥇 0.9841 (Argon) not measured not measured 0.9007 (E2B) not measured Ready in 🥇 4 s 🥇 a key 🥇 a key minutes, cold start 12–14 min minutes The Roadmap Pick by the axis that matters most, then check the others. By number of users. Users at once Start with 1, yourself Local card, or the Gemini or Token Lab free tier 2–10 Gemini API, or Cloud Run with more instances 10–64 A batching engine on your own card (vLLM, SGLang), a TPU v5e-1, or an L4 Hundreds TPU v5e-4 as four engines, or an MI300X By cost. Free first: your own card, Token Lab, and the Gemini free tier, which carries Gemma 4 26B and 31B, Flash-Lite, 3.8 Flash and Hydrogen. For paid use with light or uneven traffic, pay per token: both tests cost $0.92 on Flash-Lite and $3.46 on Argon. Hydrogen thought on every request and 3.8 Flash on most; Google's docs say reasoning cannot be turned off on Gemini 3 or Gemini 4 models, and the API runs none as low . Compare models by cost per answer. From 2026-12-01, when Carbon and Argon go to $4 / $20, this run costs $6.93 on Argon and $5.02 on Hydrogen, by arithmetic from list prices. A rented machine wins only when it is kept busy, which brings TPU v5e to $0.089 and MI300X to $0.054 per million output tokens. By speed. On a hosted API, Flash-Lite answered a GSM8K problem in 1.10 s and Hydrogen in 2.84 s; Gemma 4 on the Gemini API took 8 to 9 s. For one user, a local card with a drafter (230.5 tok/s on the 3050) or an MI300X (340.4). For many users, the MI300X or four TPU v5e chips. Cloud Run as deployed here stops at 189.53 tok/s per instance. By accuracy. Gemini 4 Argon leads GSM8K at 0.9841, and Argon and Gemma 4 31B lead BFCL at 0.9675. Where a model runs did not change its score: Gemma 4 31B answered 1,284 of 1,319 GSM8K problems through the Gemini API and 1,284 on an RTX 3050 with llama.cpp, differing on 8 problems. Model size matters more than where it runs: E2B scored 0.8954 to 0.9030 on GSM8K across six engines on the RTX 3050, the L4 and TPU v5e, and the 31B 0.9735. By ease of use. A hosted API needs a key. A local card needs a driver and an engine, and llama.cpp is ready in seconds. Cloud Run needs a container and a deploy and then scales on its own. A rented accelerator needs capacity, a 12.6 to 14.1 minute engine start on TPU, and someone to turn it off. So, Which One? Start hosted with Gemma 4 31B on the Gemini free tier: it tied the best BFCL score and costs nothing. If the task needs the best math scores, move to Gemini 4 Argon. If the task needs Gemma 4 for its open weights, privacy or offline use, run it on your own card, 12B or 31B on 8 GB. Move to Cloud Run when a few users need an always-reachable endpoint without managing a machine. Move to a TPU v5e or an MI300X when traffic is steady enough to keep it busy, because that is where the per-token cost falls below every API. Summary The goal of this article was to map where each way of running a model fits. The key to the solution was a single repo that measures local cards, hosted APIs, Cloud Run and rented accelerators with the same engines, scoring script and questions. Scope: figures come from separate runs between 2026-09-03 and 2026-11-14 in gemma4-dev, on different engine versions and days; each is quoted from its run's report, and ratios between runs on different hardware are indicative. title: Gemini 4 or Gemma 4? It Depends.
author: xbill
summary: This article provides a step by step guide to comparing the new Gemini 4 models with Gemma 4 on equal terms. Seven models, Gemma 4 26B and 31B, Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite and 3.8 Flash, and Gemini 4 Hydrogen, Carbon and Argon, run through the same Gemini API endpoint with the same questions, settings and scoring, started at the same moment. https://github.com/xbill9/gemma4-dev/tree/main/gemini-api-google-hydrogen4 The scores: on 1,319 GSM8K math problems Argon scored 0.9841, Hydrogen and Carbon 0.9803, 3.8 Flash 0.9788, Gemma 4 26B 0.9742, Gemma 4 31B 0.9735 and 3.5 Flash-Lite 0.9629. On 400 BFCL function calls Argon and Gemma 4 31B tied at 0.9675. Gemma 4 ran free; the Gemini runs cost $0.92 to $5.02. Hydrogen answered fastest of the Gemini 4 models, 2.84 s per GSM8K problem against 7.63 s for Argon. The surprise is in the cost, and it takes the whole picture to see it. Hydrogen is the cheapest Gemini 4 model per token, $7.50 per million output tokens against $10 for Carbon and Argon, and it cost the most per run, $5.02 against $3.46 for Argon. Its thinking eats the token budget: Google's docs say reasoning cannot be turned off on Gemini 4 models, it ran on all 1,319 GSM8K problems at the lowest setting, and it was 55% of the GSM8K bill. Price per token, tokens per answer and thinking per answer together set what a model costs. What Are the New Models? Gemini 4 Hydrogen, Carbon and Argon are on the Gemini API next to the 3.x Flash models and Gemma 4. title: Ship it reversible: designing the undo layer an agent's irreversible actions need
author: MapToSite
summary: The worst minute of operating an assistant was not a hallucination. It was a cheerful confirmation: "Done — I cancelled the appointment and sent the shop a note explaining why." The appointment was gone. The note was in a stranger's inbox. Neither of those is a state I can put back. There is no ctrl+z for a message someone has already read, and no version of "cancel" that returns the slot the shop had already re-let. I build an assistant that runs errands in the real world: forms, checkouts, bookings, cancellations, mail. Every design review I have with myself ends up in the same place. The interesting question is not can the agent do it . It is what does it cost to take it back , and who gets to find out. Reversibility is a property of the effect, not the verb We talk about "safe actions" as if safety lived in the API call. It does not. The same delete is a non-event on a draft and a catastrophe on the only copy of a tax document. Four things decide the class, and only one of them is in the code: Is the prior state captured somewhere? A write without a snapshot is irreversible even if the endpoint is a plain PUT . Does anyone else observe it? A message in an outbox can be edited. The same message in a stranger's inbox cannot. Irreversibility usually begins at observation , not at send. Does a second party now hold a commitment? A held table, an authorised charge, a booked slot — the shop's calendar moved. Your record is not the only copy that changed. Is there an inverse operation that is itself safe to run? A refund is an inverse of a charge. An "ignore my previous message" mail is not an inverse of a sent mail; it is a second, worse message. I now tag every effect with one of four classes before it runs: Class Meaning Example Undo cost R Reversible in place Write a field with the old value saved Milliseconds C Compensable Charge, transfer, cancel A new effect, visible to someone D Delayed Queued send, scheduled publish Free until the timer fires X Irreversible once observed Sent mail, placed call, published post None; only disclosure repair The classification takes ten minutes and changes the architecture. The agent stops treating "done" as one word. Buy reversibility with five dials Reversibility is not a boolean you find; it is something you manufacture. Five dials, in the order I reach for them. 1. Delay. Put the effect in a queue with a countdown instead of executing it. Forty seconds is enough for the person to read the confirmation line and say stop, and cheap enough that nothing else in the system notices. A delay is only honest if the countdown is visible and the item can still be withdrawn at second 39. 2. Snapshot. Before any destructive write, read the current value and store it with the effect record — not the new value, the old one. prior_state is the single field that turns most R-class mistakes into a non-event, and it is the field everybody forgets, because the happy path never reads it. 3. Stage. Split the action into a state that nobody minds and a promotion that everybody minds. A draft in the same mailbox the send would use; a preview URL that renders exactly the live page; a status='staged' row that a human or a second check promotes. Two-phase publish costs one extra state and one extra write, and it is the difference between "I posted the wrong thing" and "I staged the wrong thing". 4. Trash instead of delete. Delete sets deleted_at and hides the row; a nightly job removes it after thirty days. A tombstone is also a correct answer to "did this exist?" — which matters more than people expect when a later step needs to prove it acted on the right record. 5. Compensate. When none of the above applies, define the inverse explicitly and treat it as a first-class effect with its own record, its own approval and its own failure modes. A refund is not the absence of a charge. Most real errands need two or three of these at once: a charge with a snapshot of the prior balance, behind a delay, with a refund path defined before the charge is allowed. The record an undo needs An "undo" button is a view over a record. If the record is thin, the button lies. Minimum shape: effect = { "effect_id" : "eff_..." , # the thing that happened "action" : "cancel_booking" , "target" : "studio-4821/2026-11-20 14:00" , "class" : "C" , "prior_state" : { "status" : "confirmed" , "slot" : "2026-11-20 14:00" } , "inverse" : { "op" : "rebook" , "params" : { "slot" : "..." , "same_staff" : True } } , "window_until" : "2026-11-15T08:40:00Z" , # null when X-class "observed_by" : [ ] , # who could have seen it "status" : "applied" , # applied | undone | expired | superseded "supersedes" : None , } Three of these fields do the real work. window_until makes the undo promise finite and therefore checkable. observed_by records the moment the effect stopped being private — the earliest point at which the inverse changes meaning. supersedes is the fence: an undo that arrives after the target has moved on is not an undo, it is a new decision. Without status , an undo that failed looks identical to one that succeeded, and the next attempt is a guess. Irreversibility begins when someone else can see it This was the insight that changed how I set delays. The technical send is a write; the human event is delivery . Between those two is a variable-size gap I can use. Practical rule: the hold window must end before any second party could plausibly observe the effect. For mail, that is a matter of seconds once it leaves your provider. For a booking, it is the moment the shop's calendar re-let the slot. For a public post, it is the first crawl or the first read. For a phone call, it is the first word spoken — which is why I treat outbound calls as X-class by default and require a person to be the one who places them. Two corollaries I had to learn by breaking things: A read receipt is not a precondition for irreversibility. You do not need to know the message was read. You only need to know it can be read, which is true the instant it lands. A draft is not safe if it is auto-promoted. I once "staged" a message by writing it to the outbox provider-side, where a scheduled job I had forgotten about sent everything at 09:00. Staging must live on the side of the boundary where nothing can promote it without you. Downgrade the action instead of adding a confirmation A confirmation dialog is the cheapest possible reversibility, and the weakest: it moves the cost to the person's attention, once per action, forever. Downgrading the action removes the risk structurally. The table I keep, roughly: Raw action Reversible version What is preserved Send email Save as draft; deliver only on explicit send Recipient never sees the wrong text Book / confirm Hold, with payment and confirmation after the window Slot is not taken twice Publish page Stage + schedule, with unpublish tested Public URL never shows a wrong version Delete record Trash with tombstone and 30-day retention Recoverability and an audit trail Transfer money Reserve then settle, with a ledger line per step Reversible until settle Cancel subscription Scheduled cancellation at period end Access is not lost by accident Place call Prepare a brief; the person dials Nobody is spoken to on your behalf Submit form Save draft where the site offers one; else read-back of every field before submit Wrong values caught pre-effect Note the last row. When a site has no draft, the reversible substitute is a read-back : extract what will be submitted, compare it to what was intended, and only then press the button. It is not an undo, but it catches the majority of wrong-field errors before they become X-class. Undo is not rollback This is where I see the most confident mistakes. An inverse is a new effect with its own consequences: A refund does not erase the charge; it adds a second line the person will see, and some processors charge for it. An apology mail does not un-send the first one. It doubles the inbox traffic and usually makes the error more memorable. A re-book after a cancellation may land in a different slot with a different person, which is a different commitment from the one that existed before. Unpublishing a page does not un-index it, un-share the link, or un-read the screenshot someone took. So compensation follows the same gate as any other C-class action: it needs its terms stated, a window, and — for anything a stranger will read — a drafted text that a human releases. An automated apology is how a small slip becomes a public incident. When the undo arrives late, twice, or after the world moved The inverse is a tool call, so it inherits every tool-call problem: unknown outcomes, retries, duplicates. Three tests catch almost all of it. Twice. Undo must be idempotent against its own record. status moves applied → undone once; the second call reads undone and returns it instead of running the inverse again. Without this, an undo that timed out and was retried re-books the slot that the first undo already released. Late. After window_until , the inverse is refused and the refusal is reported, not silently downgraded. A promise you cannot keep is worse than a promise you never made; the person is planning around the sentence you printed. After the world moved. Compare the target's current state to prior_state . If it differs in the fields the inverse assumes — the row was edited, the slot was re-let, the person replied — the undo is superseded , and the right output is a question, not an action. This is the same fence that stops a stale background job from writing, applied to the reverse direction. I also test the dependency case, which is the one that hits hardest: effect A was undone while effect B was derived from it. A calendar invite derived from a cancelled booking, a receipt derived from a refunded charge. The rule I settled on is that derived effects carry the id of their cause, and undoing a cause marks its dependants orphaned for review rather than deleting them. An orphan list is a queue of questions; a silent cascade is a second incident. Test reversibility as a property, not a feature The tests that paid for themselves, all run against a scratch account: Round trip. apply then undo returns a state digest equal to the digest taken before apply . Any field that differs is either a field the inverse forgot or a field that genuinely should not return — and I want to know which. Kill in the middle. SIGKILL between the effect write and the inverse registration; restart; confirm the system can still find the effect and offer the undo. If registration is part of the same transaction, this passes for free. Undo twice. Second call returns the recorded result; the target is unchanged. Undo after edit. Mutate the target, then undo; expect superseded with the changed fields named. Window expiry. Move the clock past window_until ; expect a refusal that names the expiry, not a generic failure. Observation. Force observed_by to be non-empty; expect the system to refuse the "quiet undo" path and switch to a repair path that includes disclosure. Compensation failure. Make the inverse fail (insufficient balance, slot gone); confirm the effect stays applied with compensation_failed , and that this state is visible without anyone querying the database by hand. Test 7 is the one that turns a demo into an operating system. Most undo buttons I have used are only tested for the happy path, so the interesting states — half-undone, compensation failed, orphaned dependants — are exactly the states nobody has ever seen. What the person should see Reversibility is a promise made in the interface, so it has to be legible before the decision: The class of the action, in words: "this can be undone for 40 seconds" , "this cannot be undone" . What survives the undo: a refund line, a tombstone, a re-let slot. The exact time the window closes, not a vague "shortly". What the agent did after the window closed, if anything. And the agent should be able to say the uncomfortable sentence: "I already did the part that cannot be undone; here is what I can still do." That sentence is more useful than any success message, and it is the sentence an agent can only produce if the record told the truth about observed_by . Numbers to keep Six counters, all cheap: effects per class per day (are we shipping more X-class actions than we can watch?) undo rate per class (a rising X-class undo rate is a classification error, not a user error) windows that expired with no review (the delay is decoration if nobody reads the confirmation line) compensation failures per week orphaned dependants awaiting review median time from effect to undo, and the 95th percentile If the X-class undo rate is above zero, the fix is upstream: downgrade the action so it stops being X-class. Undo exists to cover the residual, not to make irreversible actions acceptable. Checklist Classify every effect R / C / D / X before writing the tool, and store the class on the effect record. Save prior_state on every destructive write, including the boring ones. Prefer downgrading the action over adding a confirmation dialog. Make the delay visible, finite, and withdrawable until the last second. Stage anything a stranger will read, on the side of the boundary where no scheduler can promote it. Define the inverse before allowing the action; treat compensation as a C-class effect of its own. Fence the inverse with status , window_until and a state comparison against prior_state . Mark dependants orphaned on undo instead of cascading. Test round trip, kill-mid, double undo, undo-after-edit, expiry, observation and compensation failure. Say the class and the window in the interface, before the decision. None of this makes an agent trustworthy. It makes its mistakes priced in advance — and it means the one action nobody can take back is the one the agent was never allowed to take quietly. The two links above are mine; if a sign-up completes through the invite link, both sides receive reset tickets, and the app's own notices govern any benefit. This is not a paid placement. title: What Are the Best Frameworks for Developing AI Agents?
author: Agentic Affairs
summary: What Are the Best Frameworks for Developing AI Agents? There is no best AI agent framework. There is only the framework whose lock-in you can live with — and the honest answer most vendor roundups won't give you is that the orchestration you build today is the part you will have to throw away tomorrow. Every framework on the market does the same five jobs: run the loop, call tools, keep memory, plan, and leave a trace you can inspect. What actually differs is how much of the loop they seize from you — and how painful the exit is when you outgrow them. Gartner says 40% of enterprise AI deployments will be multi-agent by 2027. That long tail is exactly why the choice matters more than the demo. The verdict, framework by framework LangGraph is the control freak's pick — and the honest one. You model the agent as an explicit graph of nodes and edges with typed state, and its durable execution is the real deal: checkpoint after every super-step, resume from a thread ID after a crash, human-in-the-loop via interrupt() . Version 1.2.20, ~44,700 stars, MIT. The catch nobody mentions: the dev server is Elastic-2.0, so you can't offer it as a managed service. Control has a price, and this one is printed in the licence. CrewAI sells you a team; AutoGen sells you a conversation. CrewAI's roles, goals and backstories map neatly onto human teams — 60,700 stars, the biggest crowd here — while AutoGen's agents argue it out in structured chat. But here's the plot twist the article buries: Microsoft already moved on. Microsoft Agent Framework hit 1.0 in April 2026 as the successor to both, and AutoGen now gets bug fixes and security patches only. If you're starting fresh on AutoGen, you're building on a framework its own maker has retired. Semantic Kernel is the proven incumbent, not the future. Microsoft's SDK for C#, Python and Java is genuinely good at wrapping existing enterprise APIs as plugins with a few lines of code. But Microsoft has told you, plainly, that Agent Framework is the path for new work. Treat Semantic Kernel as the safe choice for a .NET shop with legacy systems — not the default. The OpenAI Agents SDK is refreshingly thin — and deliberately unfinished. A handful of primitives, a Runner that handles the loop, tracing on by default. Version 0.24.0, below 1.0, interface not yet stable. Fine for a small self-hosted agent on OpenAI models; don't build your company's agent platform on a pre-1.0 API and act surprised when it moves. Google ADK is the dark horse. Code-first, model-agnostic through LiteLLM, speaks the Agent-to-Agent protocol natively, ships a real evaluation harness, deploys to Cloud Run or anywhere Python runs — not tied to Google Cloud despite the name. Version 2.14.1, Apache 2.0. The most complete package here that nobody is hyping. LlamaIndex is the data-first answer — and only that. If your agent's job is answering over your own documents, its retrieval-grounded agents and FaithfulnessEvaluator are the right tool. If the job is mostly acting, you're using a screwdriver as a hammer. The part everyone skips: price the exit Prompts, plain-function tools and evaluation cases will probably carry over. The orchestration won't — a LangGraph graph, a CrewAI crew and an AutoGen group chat are built on different models, and checkpoint formats don't travel. Assess each part for reuse before you commit, not after you're locked in. Match the framework to the job: solo assistant, go OpenAI Agents SDK or LangGraph for long jobs that must survive restarts. Team of specialists, CrewAI for roles or Microsoft Agent Framework for critique-and-revise. Enterprise workflow, Semantic Kernel for .NET, Google ADK for Google Cloud, LlamaIndex for retrieval over internal docs.
